name: HCP Vault Radar
license: Proprietary: an HCP software-as-a-service; the `vault-radar` CLI and agent ship as closed-source binaries under a HashiCorp licence agreement
summary: A hosted scanner that finds leaked secrets and personal data in code, wikis, tickets and chat, checks which ones still work, and helps move them into Vault.
intro: Vault Radar is a service in the HashiCorp Cloud Platform (HCP). You connect data sources, such as a GitHub organization, a Confluence site or a Slack workspace, and Radar scans each one in full when it is added, then again on every new commit and pull request. Short-lived scan workers, isolated per project, clone the minimum they need into a temporary directory and look for about 330 secret types, personal data (PII) and non-inclusive language, using patterns, entropy and Base64 decoding. Radar doesn’t keep the secrets it finds: it hashes each value with Argon2id and a per-customer salt, then with a per-project HMAC key, and stores only that hash and where it was found. For sources HCP can’t reach, you run the agent, part of the `vault-radar` CLI, on Kubernetes or a Linux host in your network. It polls HCP for jobs, scans with credentials that stay local, and uploads only metadata.

What it adds to plain pattern matching is triage. For about 120 secret types Radar calls the issuing service to see whether the secret still works, and it ranks a finding critical when the secret is active and still in the latest version of a file or page, high when it is active but only in history, and low for PII. When the agent is connected to Vault Enterprise or HCP Vault Dedicated, Radar indexes Vault’s KV secrets as hashes and marks leaks that match a secret Vault manages, and from the findings list you can copy a leaked value into a Vault KV path before rotating it. The CLI also runs on its own, in CI pipelines, as a pre-commit hook, or against folders, Docker images, AWS Parameter Store and HCP Terraform variables. Radar grew out of BluBracket, a secret-scanning startup HashiCorp bought in June 2023, and became generally available in April 2025.
strengths: Looks beyond git: Confluence, Jira, Slack, Microsoft Teams, Amazon S3, Docker images, AWS Parameter Store and HCP Terraform variables end up in one inventory
Ranks findings by whether the secret still works and is still in the latest version, so triage starts with live leaks
Ties into Vault: flags leaked copies of secrets Vault manages and copies leaked values into Vault KV as a first remediation step
The hybrid agent keeps data-source credentials and content inside your network; HCP only receives hashes and metadata
Pull request checks, pre-commit hooks and CI commands for GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps
limits: Proprietary and tied to HCP: there is no self-hosted control plane, and the agent and most CLI scans need an HCP project, which supplies the salt for hashing findings
Vault correlation and copying secrets into Vault need Vault Enterprise or HCP Vault Dedicated; Vault Community Edition isn’t supported
The free trial covers 2 data sources and 100 resources, with only built-in patterns and Jira and Slack integrations; anything larger needs the paid Essentials tier
Fewer detectors than the free TruffleHog: about 330 built-in secret types (Base64 variants included), about 120 with a live check
Hard limits and betas: repositories over 2 GB aren’t scanned, a GitHub connection covers 5,000 repositories, and SharePoint, OneDrive, EC2, EBS and HCP Terraform variable scans are beta

snippet.title: Scan a repository’s history against a Vault index, then block new leaks at commit time
source: # A service principal with the Vault Radar CLI User role in your HCP project
# Hash every KV v2 secret version in Vault into a local index (beta)
# Clone and scan every reachable commit; findings that match a Vault secret show its Vault path
export VAULT_RADAR_GIT_TOKEN=...   # a GitHub token that can clone the repo
# Reject commits that add a finding of high severity or worse
vault-radar install git pre-commit-hook   # needs a Vault Radar licence

sections.title: Vault Radar or a free scanner?
sections.intro: GitHub, gitleaks and TruffleHog all find secrets in git for free or close to it. Radar’s case rests on the sources outside git, the ranking, and the tie-in with Vault.

notes: If your code lives on GitHub and your leaks would be in code, GitHub’s own scanning plus push protection covers most of the ground. Radar earns its price when secrets also leak into wikis, tickets and chat, or when you already run Vault Enterprise and want leaks matched against it.
The gitleaks maintainer has declared it feature complete: future releases are security patches only.

items.name: HCP scanning
items.text: Radar’s own workers in HCP clone and scan sources reachable from the internet. Simplest to set up; HCP holds the data-source credentials in its secrets manager.

items.name: Agent
items.text: `vault-radar agent exec` in a Kubernetes deployment or on a Linux host. It polls HCP for scan jobs and keeps credentials local; needed for on-premises sources and for Vault correlation and copying.

items.name: CLI
items.text: The same binary scans a repo, folder, Docker image or Parameter Store on demand, runs `scan ci pr` in a pipeline, and installs a pre-commit hook. Most scans need HCP credentials so hashes match across runs.

items.name: Editor and AI tools
items.text: A VS Code extension highlights secrets when a file is opened or saved and can copy them into Vault, without talking to HCP. An MCP server lets an AI assistant query a project’s data sources and findings.

story: A secrets manager protects only the secrets that are put into it. The rest end up in source code, wikis, tickets and chat, where anyone who can read them can use them. BluBracket, a Palo Alto start-up led by co-founder and CEO Prakash Linga, sold scanning for secrets hidden in “source code, development environments, internal websites, chat services, ticketing systems, and other locations.” HashiCorp announced it had acquired BluBracket on June 27, 2023. HashiCorp’s James Bayer explained why: “we’ve never had the capability to discover and find secrets and then import them into Vault.”

The scanner was rebuilt as a service in HCP and opened as an alpha, HCP Vault Radar, at HashiConf in October 2023. A limited beta followed in January 2024 and limited availability in March; by then Radar checked whether Google Cloud, AWS and GitHub credentials were live and matched findings against Vault. HashiCorp raised the severity of leaks that match a Vault secret because “Most credentials in Vault are used in critical production environments.”

Radar became generally available on April 30, 2025, two months after IBM completed its purchase of HashiCorp, with the ability to copy discovered secrets straight into Vault. The beta matched leaks against Vault Community Edition too; the current documentation limits that to Vault Enterprise and HCP Vault Dedicated.

choices.choice: Keep a hash of each finding, never the secret
choices.why: A database of every leaked credential would be a target in itself. Radar stores an Argon2id hash, HMACed with a per-project key, so recovering a value needs the original source; matching against Vault works by comparing hashes.

choices.choice: Rank by whether the secret works and is still current
choices.why: Scanners that only match patterns drown teams in test keys and long-dead credentials. Radar weighs version history, entropy and a live check to put active secrets in current files at the top.

choices.choice: A hybrid agent that only calls out
choices.why: Many repositories and wikis sit behind firewalls, and security teams don’t want a SaaS holding their credentials. The agent polls HCP for jobs from inside the network, so no inbound access is needed and credentials never leave it.

choices.choice: Check findings against the secrets manager
choices.why: A leaked value that also lives in Vault is probably a production credential. Matching the two tells a team what to rotate first and where the managed copy is.
